title: Raheem Sterling · who gets judged?
summary: Compare the criticised property framing with reports about Sterling’s challenge.
supportedFinding: Ask whether an outlet originates, amplifies, challenges or contextualises a hostile frame. Racially unequal framing can be examined without guessing private motives.
limits: Two historical headline reproductions and two reaction reports are a limited sample. They do not prove that every article, journalist or reader shared the same motive.
caseComparisonNote: Two stories are earlier headline reproductions; two report the later public criticism. Different people, dates and genres prevent a perfectly controlled comparison. Both reproduced property headlines come from one outlet.

evidence.text: Sterling publicly contrasted coverage of Tosin Adarabioyo and Phil Foden buying homes. He argued that the framing of young Black players contributed to racism. This is his attributed criticism, not a regulator’s finding.
evidence.label: Contemporaneous report and reproduced Instagram images

evidence.text: The cited comparison concerns property-purchase framing. The two examples concern different people and were published at different times; full original article context and live original pages are missing from this packet.
evidence.label: Contemporaneous statement transcript and context

evidence.text: The current Editors’ Code recognises public-interest reporting while requiring proportionality, accuracy, privacy and care around discrimination. It is a learning framework here, not a finding that a particular outlet breached a rule. Historical articles must be judged against their own context and applicable rules.
evidence.label: IPSO Editors’ Code: public interest and proportionality

reasoningChecks.prompt: What is the direct comparison here?

options.label: Two home-purchase headlines with contrasting emphasis
Two identical articles apart from race
An upheld regulator finding against every outlet

reasoningChecks.explanation: The difference in wording is observable. It is a reason to investigate unequal treatment; it does not prove all surrounding circumstances identical.

reasoningChecks.prompt: Are the reaction reports the original criticised stories?

options.label: No: reporting the complaint is a different contribution
Yes: all four published the original property stories
Reaction coverage can never amplify harm

reasoningChecks.explanation: Separate originating a frame, repeating it without context and reporting criticism of it. Each can affect a campaign differently.

options.label: Different people/dates, reproduced headlines, incomplete original context
This is a complete census of all coverage
The difference in wording cannot matter

reasoningChecks.explanation: An incomplete sample can raise a substantive concern without establishing the prevalence or intention of an outlet’s whole output.

options.label: Testing evidence about conduct or institutions
Lots of people want to click
A famous person has no privacy

reasoningChecks.explanation: Popularity alone does not justify intrusion. Ask what the reporting helps the public understand and whether its treatment is proportionate.

reasoningChecks.prompt: What can this packet establish about private motives?

options.label: Framing can be assessed; private motives remain unproved
Every journalist intended to bully
All motives were harmless

reasoningChecks.explanation: Observable stereotyping, repetition or ridicule can be criticised without claiming to know every journalist’s intention or every reader’s feelings.

title: Caroline Flack · scrutiny or spectacle?
summary: Weigh reporting of proceedings against a wider pattern of scrutiny.
supportedFinding: A legitimate reason to report an allegation does not settle the proportionality of the coverage surrounding it.
limits: This sample cannot establish an outlet’s whole campaign, private motives or a causal explanation for a death. Judge publication choices regardless of later consequences.
caseComparisonNote: These pieces span charge reporting, court reporting and later media review. They are not simultaneous or a complete record of any outlet’s output.

evidence.text: The CPS’s later account records a not-guilty plea and a planned trial. The proceedings did not deliver a trial verdict. The CPS maintains that bringing the prosecution was appropriate; that is its institutional position, not a finding that every news treatment was justified.
evidence.label: CPS case statement, 10 November 2025

evidence.text: Researchers categorised 387 newspaper reports; the analysis does not establish causation.
evidence.label: Published coverage-count analysis

evidence.text: The current Editors’ Code recognises public-interest reporting while requiring proportionality, accuracy, privacy and care around discrimination. It is a learning framework here, not a finding that a particular outlet breached a rule. Historical articles must be judged against their own context and applicable rules.
evidence.label: IPSO Editors’ Code: public interest and proportionality

options.label: A charge and a not-guilty plea, not a trial conviction
A trial proved guilt
No charge could ever be newsworthy

reasoningChecks.explanation: Accountability reporting must retain the difference between an allegation and a verdict. A later statement must not be treated as information every editor had in 2019.

reasoningChecks.prompt: What does the coverage count support?

options.label: A described pattern in a sampled set of reports
Proof that one headline caused her death
Proof that every story was hostile

reasoningChecks.explanation: Counts help investigate repetition and tone. They do not settle the propriety of every article or establish a sole cause.

title: Jason Arday · accountability or humiliation?
summary: Examine investigation, ridicule, racial spillover and later media reflection.
supportedFinding: Legitimate academic scrutiny and harmful racialised amplification can coexist. Judge what an outlet contributes, how it frames the person and whether it turns one case into a stereotype.
limits: This packet supplies institutional statements and four pieces, not a completed independent finding on every allegation or a causal explanation for his death.
caseComparisonNote: Opinion, a resignation report, an explainer and later debate appear at different stages. Evaluate added facts, repetition and tone at each publication date; this is not a complete campaign census.

evidence.text: On 12 August Cambridge announced an investigation into the circumstances of the appointment and his time at the university. Institutional accountability is a real issue; announcing an investigation does not itself establish its findings.
evidence.label: Cambridge Vice-Chancellor statement, 12 August 2026

evidence.text: On 21 August Cambridge condemned racist and hateful messages being received by Black students and staff and members of its education faculty. That documents wider harm, not that every report caused it or every journalist intended it.
evidence.label: Cambridge community statement, 21 August 2026

evidence.text: The opinion headline presents an ongoing controversy as entertainment. Decide whether its tone is proportionate to the accountability issue; a headline alone is a limited sample of the writer’s argument.
evidence.label: Original commentary, dated 31 July 2026

evidence.text: The current Editors’ Code recognises public-interest reporting while requiring proportionality, accuracy, privacy and care around discrimination. It is a learning framework here, not a finding that a particular outlet breached a rule. Historical articles must be judged against their own context and applicable rules.
evidence.label: IPSO Editors’ Code: public interest and proportionality

reasoningChecks.prompt: What is a legitimate scrutiny question?

options.label: How an institution appointed and reviewed a researcher
Whether one case proves a minority unfit for academia
Any scrutiny of a vulnerable person is forbidden

reasoningChecks.explanation: Institutional due diligence and research integrity can warrant investigation. That does not justify humiliation or generalising about an ethnic group.

reasoningChecks.prompt: What wider harm is documented here?

options.label: Racist and hateful messages reported by the university
Proof of every journalist’s private racial motive
A final finding about all allegations

reasoningChecks.explanation: The university’s statement documents hostile messages to a wider community. Attribution and causal limits still matter.

reasoningChecks.prompt: What should guide your assessment of earlier coverage?

Any repeated story automatically proves harassment

reasoningChecks.explanation: Consequences matter to reflection, but they do not replace judging each editorial contribution, chronology and what is supported.
